Title: Distributed Collaboration between Industry and University Partners in Higher Education

Authors: Erik Bohemia*, Neil Smith**, Kerry Harman***, Trevor Duncan****, Chris Turnock*****, and Sung-Gul Hwang******

* School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom. Email: erik.bohemia@northumbria.ac.uk

** School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom. Email: neil.smith@northumbria.ac.uk

Abstract: In the last three years, the School of Design has tried out a new approach to curriculum design and delivery called ‘the Global Studio’. This initiative involves a research-driven teaching and learning partnership across institutions, including Northumbria University, international universities, and industry partners in the UK, USA, Netherlands, and Korea. The Global Studio aims to meet the current and future demands of the industry, particularly in areas undergoing shifts in how products and services are developed. These industry changes stress the need for design students to learn how to work in globally connected organizations, focusing on enhancing intercultural communication and collaboration skills. This paper highlights the Global Studio activities of 2008, which involved Northumbria University (UK), Hongik University (Korea), Auburn University (USA), Intel (USA), Motorola design studios in the UK and Korea, and Great Southern Wood (USA). The discussion will showcase both the hurdles and benefits of undertaking international collaborative projects within distributed environments.

Keywords: Global Studio; Industry-Based Projects; International Collaboration.
Over the last three years, the School of Design at Northumbria University has been experimenting with an innovative curriculum approach known as 'the Global Studio'. This initiative is a collaboration in teaching and learning that is informed by research and conducted jointly with other universities and industry partners worldwide. The participating institutions in this project are TU Delft, Napier University, Hongik University, Ohio State University, Auburn University, and RMIT University, along with corporations like Intel, Motorola, Great Southern Wood, and Inverness Medical Innovation. These organizations are based in the UK, USA, Netherlands, Australia, and Korea. The objectives of the Global Studio align with both current and anticipated industry demands, specifically addressing changes in how products and services are developed. These shifts underscore the necessity for design students to be equipped with skills tailored for working within globally networked organizations, focusing particularly on intercultural communication and collaboration skills. This paper centers on the 2008 iteration of the Global Studio. It will briefly introduce the collaborative projects between Northumbria University and its industry partners in the USA and Korea. Following this, we will examine the interaction and communication among project teams. Our analysis is based on evaluation data gathered from students in the UK while the projects were ongoing and upon their completion. Additionally, insights from two authors who were involved in delivering the Global Studio contribute to the data set.
The initial Global Studio was imagined as a course held annually, involving universities from various countries. One of the primary goals of the Global Studio was to create a learning space where students could cultivate skills in intercultural communication and collaboration, while being cost-effective so that the entire group of students could take part. Another objective was to develop a framework allowing each partner university to handle teaching and assessment independently, thus addressing some challenges of inter-institutional collaborations [1]. In the beginning course, student roles and associated tasks were organized throughout to promote cross-institutional communication and interaction, mainly by having students serve as both client and designer. An extensive explanation of how the client and designer roles were structured is available elsewhere [1]. A year afterward, a different program in the School of Design adopted the Global Studio with the aim not only of collaborating with university partners but also of engaging with industry partners situated in various locales. The involvement of industry partners introduced further challenges compared to the prior Global Studio. For instance, the presence of industry partners complicated the dynamics of interaction and communication among students, faculty, and industry partners (see Figure 1 and Figure 2). Figure 1. Interactions between student teams and lecturers in the Global Studio conducted in 20072 1 Only students based in the UK completed the project exit surveys, so the data largely reflect the views of Northumbria University students unless specified otherwise. 2 Note: There were several work teams situated at each partner university 236 Figure 2. Increased complexity of interactions between student teams, industry partners, and lecturers in the Global Studio conducted in 20082 The addition of three industry partners also influenced how projects were organized and impacted student roles and activities. In the 2008 Global Studio, for example, industry partners assumed the role of clients. Consequently, students from participating universities no longer acted as ‘clients’ and ‘designers’ for one another as they did in the previous Global Studio. This significantly altered how students from various universities interacted and communicated with one another.
In this section, we'll give a brief overview of the industry-focused projects undertaken during the 2008 Global Studio. Three collaborative industry projects were part of the Global Studio: ‘Constructing Constructs’, ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, and ‘On the Move’. Each project involved various industry and university partners (refer to Table 1). The ‘Constructing Constructs’ initiative was a joint effort between Northumbria University and Hong-ik University in Korea, working alongside Motorola's design studios in the UK and Korea. A staff member from Motorola's Korean Design office also taught an elective class for 10 third-year industrial design students at the Korean university. This project focused on exploring the sub-themes of ‘Constructing Luxury’ and ‘Constructing Technology’ [3]. The second project, ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, engaged universities in the UK and the USA in partnership with Great Southern Wood, a national timber company in the USA. Auburn University’s final-year industrial design students participated, and the project was coordinated by a lecturer based there. Intel, a major semiconductor company, commissioned the ‘On the Move’ project, conducted between Northumbria University and their USA office. This project explored three fundamental sub-themes: ‘Design for Experience’, ‘Imagining a Notebook’, and ‘Futures of Mobile Computing’. All projects included participation from a third-year class of 34 Industrial Design students from Northumbria University. Students chose their preferred project, with ten opting for ‘On the Move’, twelve for ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, and another twelve for ‘Constructing Constructs’. Additionally, several Master of Design students observed these project teams as part of their Design Management studies. Although not directly involved in the design work, undergraduate students appreciated having them shadow the teams, citing their presence as a ‘wealth of knowledge’. Each principal project group was also divided into smaller work teams. For ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, six work teams were formed at each participating university. The ‘Constructing Constructs’ project comprised three linked teams at each university. 

Table 1. Global Studio Work Teams and Partners Industry-Based Projects: Constructing Constructs Northumbria University (UK) 3 groups, 4 members per group Hong-ik University (Korea) 3 groups, 3 members per group Motorola, a multinational mobile phone manufacturer (UK and Korea) Thinking Outside the Box Northumbria University (UK) 6 groups, 2 members per group Auburn University (USA) 6 groups, 2 members per group Great Southern Wood, a national USA timber company On the Move Northumbria University (UK) 10 to 7 students Intel, a multinational semiconductor company (USA) Students working on the ‘On the Move’ project developed individual concepts. However, they were encouraged to collaborate in pairs during various stages of the design process, such as idea generation. This cohort was also asked to present their work collectively to the industry partner, rather than individually pitching their ideas.
The 'On the Move' initiative kicked off with an industry representative visiting Northumbria University and introducing the project team to three main sub-themes: 'Design for Experience,' 'Imagining a Notebook,' and 'Futures of Mobile Computing.' Each sub-theme was intended to propose a design solution within a distinct time frame. 'Design for Experience’ focused on current solutions, 'Imagining a Notebook' targeted ideas looking four years ahead, and 'Futures of Mobile Computing' took an even longer-term perspective. Students were instructed to interpret the guidelines and present a brief for discussion with industry representatives. The only restriction was that the screen size of any proposed device could not fall below the company’s specified minimum. Throughout the project, industry partners from 'On the Move' consistently visited Northumbria University for in-person meetings and project evaluations. The sub-themes determined by the Motorola representative spanned two major themes: 'New Luxury' (Constructing Luxury) and 'New Digital Lifestyle' (Constructing Technology). A teleconference connected universities in the UK and Korea with industry partner representatives for a briefing session that included a presentation. The sole request from the industry representative was to exclude phones from the design proposals. Initially, this caused confusion among team members since they assumed the project would involve the company’s typical product range, such as mobile phones. Once more, student groups were tasked with creating a design brief based on one of the two sub-themes. A briefing session for the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project was led by a lecturer from Auburn University, who coordinated this industry project. Student teams from Northumbria University collaborated with teams from Auburn University. The UK students were asked to develop a design brief that would enhance the work being done by their American counterparts.
After attending the briefing sessions, students were instructed to upload an introduction along with a photo of themselves onto the project wiki pages. Next, the work teams were tasked with creating a shared space for their team that included: (i) a wiki page, (ii) a team name, (iii) a logo, and (iv) uploading design briefs onto their team project wiki pages. This activity was followed by a virtual meeting with other partners to discuss the design briefs. Once the briefs were finalized, the teams conducted research to explore different ways to address the design briefs. The research findings were evaluated to aid in developing concepts, which were then reviewed to guide further refinements and iterations of the design proposals. This process culminated in a presentation of the final design proposal to representatives from the industry partners. The presentation formats varied among the project workgroups. For instance, the 'On the Move' final design proposals were presented as a series of 2-minute animations highlighting the key benefits of each design concept, which were compiled into a standalone DVD presentation. The 'Constructing Constructs' presentation comprised storyboards mixed with multimedia animation. Meanwhile, 'Thinking Outside the Box' included both storyboards and scaled-down models to illustrate the operational principles of different design ideas. The three projects employed various communication tools to facilitate both asynchronous and synchronous interactions. The choice of these tools was guided by the communication resources available at each participating partner organization and the IT policies of the UK-based university. Students were given the chance to work both in collocated and distributed environments and engage through various communication technologies for synchronous and asynchronous interactions. For instance, they collaborated in person and communicated synchronously with team members stationed at the same institution (depicted in the top left quadrant of Figure 3). These team members also utilized asynchronous communication tools like email and wiki pages (shown in the top right quadrant of Figure 3). They operated in distributed settings, communicating synchronously through tele/videoconferencing with partners situated in different geographic areas (illustrated in the bottom left quadrant of Figure 3). For asynchronous communication with partners in other locations, they relied on email and wiki pages (indicated in the bottom right quadrant of Figure 3).
To facilitate asynchronous communication, each project was given secure, dedicated wiki pages using MediaWiki software. These pages were hosted by Northumbria University. Several reasons led to the selection of wiki pages as a communication tool:

1. External collaborators could access these specific project wiki pages, while the university's existing online learning platform (Blackboard) was limited to enrolled students and university staff. 
   
2. Users with individual log-ins enjoyed unlimited access to create, edit, and link pages, offering flexibility in organizing their group or individual project wiki pages.
   
3. Basic text editing in wikis did not require HTML coding knowledge, and standard files could be uploaded, so there was no need for special external software like web editors or FTP clients.

The intention was for the design teams to upload their work, such as design briefs, research materials including mind maps, mood boards, and videos, sketches and other visual interpretations of design concepts, storyboards, and multimedia files like animations and movies onto their group or individual project wiki pages. Participants at each site could then view these pages during scheduled synchronous project meetings, allowing them to present and review the project using the material available on the wiki pages.
While all students participated in the introductory exercise, many struggled with using the wiki pages. Some chose not to use them at all, particularly those from Auburn University, who opted for Facebook for asynchronous communication with their UK counterparts instead of the designated project wiki pages. Consequently, UK students involved in the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project also switched to using Facebook over the wiki pages. One UK student remarked, "I enjoyed video/tele conferencing, which taught me new skills and boosted my confidence in presenting my ideas through different methods. However, the student I partnered with didn't use the wiki pages despite my persistent requests. Therefore, I didn't contribute much as I feared it would go unnoticed." 

The USA-based students highlighted issues with frequently overwriting each other's wiki pages, files, and images, as one comment reveals: "The wiki page was a pain. Loading images was a nightmare. Since our class wasn't familiar with the system, many students misplaced pages and overwrote others' work." A technical explanation for this is that wiki pages have a 'flat' structure, unlike HTML-based web pages with folders. This means each new wiki page, image, or file must have a unique name, or it risks overwriting existing content. For instance, if a student uploaded a photo titled 'my photo.jpg', and another student uploaded a photo with the same name, a warning would appear indicating the name conflict, but if they proceeded, the previous image would be overwritten. The outcome of their actions wouldn't be apparent unless they viewed the affected wiki pages. 

Students consistently criticized the wiki's cumbersome editing interface, inadequate file-uploading capabilities, and slow upload speed. To address these issues, teams working on the 'Constructing Constructs' project uploaded large multimedia files to free file-sharing websites and shared the links on their project wiki pages so others could access them. This approach, however, created new challenges. For one, project files were no longer hosted in a secure environment, potentially compromising confidentiality. Additionally, the shared links often expired after a few days. Other concerns included advertisements for adult content and malicious software on these free sites, which could infect visitors' computers. 

Despite these obstacles, students appreciated having a web space for sharing project progress, as one commented, "Wiki pages can be confusing, but it's beneficial to have a place to share ideas and work." They also noted that making their work, such as multimedia files, available online to other student teams and industry partners facilitated communication, allowing them to explain ideas via phone or videoconference. Furthermore, observing others' work and being observed themselves added a competitive element, as highlighted by a student's comment: "Seeing the competition pushes you to work to your fullest potential. Engaging with others enhances your work."
During the 2008 Global Studio, the UK-based university had IT policies that restricted the use of all messaging and Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) software. This policy prevented faculty and students from using internet-based software for synchronous communication, such as AOL Messenger, MSN Messenger, Yahoo! Messenger, Net Meeting, ooVoo, and Skype, with external collaborators through the university's IT infrastructure. Consequently, participants had to rely on traditional phones or videoconferencing equipment for real-time communication. Teleconferencing was employed to facilitate synchronous discussions between those involved in the 'Constructing Constructs' and the 'On the Move' projects, with industry partners providing the resources and setting up these meetings, which often lasted two hours or more. Each session cost roughly £100. For example, a Motorola representative based in the UK organized a three-way teleconference bridge, enabling meetings among the UK and Korean universities and the industry partner. The presence of standard videoconferencing equipment at the UK and USA universities allowed frequent video meetings between work teams spanning these institutions. Since only university phones and videoconferencing devices could be utilized, both lecturers and industry partners had to plan these synchronous meetings well ahead of time. This plan meant that while the UK students remained in the university, where they usually worked, impromptu discussions with external partners were unlikely unless they were willing to shoulder high personal phone bills. Student teams mainly relying on teleconferencing for synchronous discussions, along with wiki pages for collaboration ('Constructing Constructs' and 'On the Move'), noted that videoconferencing might have better facilitated their ability to convey ideas and showcase concepts. They also raised concerns about the sound quality of speakerphones. Conversely, the 'Thinking Outside the Box' teams, who primarily relied on videoconferencing while opting not to use project wiki pages, mentioned difficulties in visualizing concepts during video meetings. Teams working on the 'On the Move' project had several face-to-face interactions with industry partners throughout the project (see Table 3), though only one student mentioned the significance of these encounters. The availability and adoption of communication technologies among project teams varied (see Table 2).

All the industry-related projects kicked off in February. However, the ‘On the Move’ project wrapped up 2½ months later than the other two. Table 3 outlines how often communication meetings occurred for these projects and their respective durations. It also highlights the technology used for communication and whether industry partners participated. For instance, industry partners attended all communication sessions for the ‘Constructing the Construct’ and ‘On the Move’ projects. In contrast, the partner for ‘Thinking Outside the Box’ didn’t join the UK-based teams until the project’s latter half. Notably, this was the only project where video conferencing was employed for meetings. Teams involved with the 'On the Move' project held nine meetings over a 20-week period with industry partners. Four of these were in-person when the U.S.-based staff visited the UK team. During the 10 weeks of the ‘Constructing the Construct’ project, teams met seven times with both university and industry partners. Similarly, teams working on ‘Thinking Outside the Box’ held an equal number of meetings over the same period, mostly via videoconferencing, but only two included the industry partner.

Students on the ‘Thinking Outside the Box’ project found their experience less satisfying compared to those on the other two projects, rating the success of project phases such as writing a design brief, communicating design concepts, reviewing design progress, and presenting final proposals lower. Conversely, over 80% of students from the other two projects rated each phase as either ‘very well’ or ‘well’ executed. Despite this, students from 'Thinking Outside the Box' acknowledged that their participation in the Global Studio improved their long-distance communication skills and highlighted challenges of distributed communication with comments like: "It has made me realize how difficult it is to communicate across countries," and, "First time using Wiki pages and video conferencing; now I know why it’s so blooming difficult!" These themes resonated with students from the other projects too, who reported increased confidence in public speaking and idea presentation using diverse communication technologies. A student from the ‘On the Move’ project said: "my confidence in discussing ideas with people from different countries has increased," and another mentioned, "I have more confidence with my communication skills due to the weekly meetings." 

Overall, students felt the course enhanced their ability to communicate over distances, and the vast majority credited the Global Studio with providing a better understanding of working with distributed design teams or clients. Korean students noted that the Global Studio offered a chance to practice and improve their English. Most students had positive learning experiences and recognized the educational benefits of the Global Studio, for instance: "Through this project, I gained experiential learning which enhanced my free thinking, confidence, and willingness to challenge," "I learned how easily communication over the internet can fail," "Communicating online without body language was a significant challenge for me," "I became aware of the difficulties in long-distance communication," "I developed my skills in using various communication media," "Interacting with a real client was beneficial, and teamwork with Korean students improved," "Learning to provide comprehensive descriptions both online and in person without prior context improved my communication skills," and, "I realized how much I rely on verbal explanation."
Overall, students reported that they enjoyed the learning experience offered through the Global Studio. They unanimously felt that their communication skills improved from collaborating with both international universities and industry partners. However, they also mentioned difficulties with communication technologies, particularly the wiki pages. A study titled ‘The Great Expectations of ICT’ [6] examined first-year students' experiences with ICT in the UK Higher Education sector and found that students are both unfamiliar with and uncomfortable using wiki pages. This report argues that this technology currently pushes students "beyond their comfort zones" [7]. Findings from the Global Studio suggest a need for improved training and accessible tutorials throughout the project to help students with the wiki pages. Alternatively, external wiki editors could be considered to simplify the editing process. The academic team at Northumbria University is also collaborating closely with IT and Learning Technology staff to determine what support is needed to enhance communication across the distributed teams in the Global Studio. This multidisciplinary research team is actively exploring technologies that would allow student groups to initiate teleconferences or videoconferences with their peers at other universities. Data also indicated that frequent videoconferencing between UK and USA student teams did not result in increased student satisfaction. These students reported the least satisfaction on most progress and exit survey indicators. Additionally, the industry partner did not engage with the UK teams until the mid-project progress review, which may have contributed to their dissatisfaction. From the lecturers' perspective, managing three industry projects was complex, leading to the decision to undertake only one industry project in subsequent Global Studios to simplify communication and management. In conclusion, we believe that the Global Studio offers students a rich learning environment by exposing them to the complexities of communication and project management in distributed settings with international university and industry partners.
